concepts.title: Generative Models
concepts.one_liner: Generative models are stochastic functions that map labels or descriptions to data, performing the synthesis of data in a one-to-many fashion.
concepts.content:
Generative models perform or describe the synthesis of data. While an image classifier is a many-to-one function $f: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{Y}$ mapping images to labels, a generative model is a function in the opposite direction $g: \mathcal{Y} \rightarrow \mathcal{X}$. Because there are many possible outputs for any given input (one-to-many), generative models handle this ambiguity by treating $g$ as a stochastic function.

(see figure: A generator maps labels (or other descriptions) to images.)
concepts.motivation_md: Generative models allow us to create new data samples and understand the underlying distribution of a dataset, which is useful for tasks like image synthesis and data augmentation.
concepts.recap_md: - Generative models map labels or descriptions to data (synthesis).

concepts.title: Generator Stochastic Function
concepts.one_liner: A generator is a function that produces stochastic outputs by mapping a randomized input vector and an optional label to a deterministic output.
concepts.content:
One way to make a function stochastic is to make it a deterministic function of a stochastic input. We define $g$ as a function, called a **generator**, that takes a randomized vector $\mathbf{z}$ as input along with the label/description $\mathbf{y}$, and produces an image $\mathbf{x}$ as output, that is, $g: \mathcal{Z} \times \mathcal{Y} \rightarrow \mathcal{X}$. Then this function can output a different image $\mathbf{x}$ for each different setting of $\mathbf{z}$. The generative process is as follows: first sample $\mathbf{z}$ from a prior $p(Z)$, then deterministically generate an image based on $\mathbf{z}$ and $\mathbf{y}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}    \mathbf{z} \sim p(Z)\\
    \mathbf{x} = g(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{y})
\end{aligned}
$$

By treating the generator as a deterministic function of a random 'noise' vector, we can produce a diverse set of outputs from a single learned mapping.

concepts.title: Latent Variables
concepts.one_liner: Latent variables are unobserved inputs that specify attributes of the generated data not determined by the label.
concepts.content: Usually we draw $\mathbf{z}$ from a simple distribution such as Gaussian noise, that is, $p(Z) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{1})$. The way to think of $\mathbf{z}$ is that it is a vector of **latent variables**, which specify all the attributes of the images other than those determined by the label. These variables are called latent because they are not directly observed in the training data (it just consists of images $\mathbf{x}$ and their labels $\mathbf{y}$). In our example, $\mathbf{y}$ tells $g$ to make a bird but the $\mathbf{z}$-vector is what specifies exactly which bird. Different dimensions of $\mathbf{z}$ specify different attributes, such as the size, color, pose, background, and so on; everything necessary to fully determine the output image.
concepts.motivation_md: Training data often lacks explicit labels for every possible visual detail (like lighting or pose). Latent variables provide a mathematical way to represent these hidden factors, allowing the model to account for all the variation present in the real data.
concepts.recap_md: - Latent variables are not directly observed in the training data.

concepts.title: Unconditional Generative Model
concepts.one_liner: An unconditional generative model produces data from scratch by modeling the distribution $p(X)$ without dependency on an input label.
concepts.content:
Sometimes we wish to simply make up data from scratch; in fact, this is the canonical setting in which generative models are often studied. To do so, we can simply drop the dependency on the input $\mathbf{y}$. This yields a procedure for making data from scratch:

$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{z} \sim p(Z)\\
    \mathbf{x} = g(\mathbf{z})
\end{aligned}$$

concepts.motivation_md: Unconditional models are useful when we want to learn the general structure of a dataset without needing specific labels, or when the goal is to synthesize entirely new examples that belong to a general category.

concepts.title: Conditional Generative Model
concepts.one_liner: A conditional generative model is a model of a conditional distribution $p(X | Y)$.
concepts.content: A **conditional generative model** is a model of any conditional distribution $p(X \bigm | Y)$. These models focus on generating data $\mathbf{x}$ given a specific input or label $\mathbf{y}$.
concepts.motivation_md: In many applications, we don't just want a random image; we want an image of a specific thing (like a 'cat' or a 'dog'). Conditional models allow us to control the output of the generation process using external information.
concepts.recap_md: - Models the conditional distribution $p(X | Y)$.

concepts.title: Content Creation: Procedural Rivers
concepts.one_liner: Generative models can be used for content creation, such as procedurally generating landscapes or river paths in video games.
concepts.content:
One reason to use unconditional generative models is content creation. Suppose we are making a video game and we want to automatically generate a bunch of exciting levels for the player to explore. We would like a procedure for making up new levels from scratch. Such procedures have been successfully used to generate random landscapes and cities for virtual realities. Suppose we want to add a river to a landscape. We need to decide what path the river should take. A simple program for generating the path could be "walk an increment forward, flip a coin to decide whether to turn left or right, repeat."

concepts.title: Sampling from a Generative Model
concepts.one_liner: Sampling is the process of querying a learned generator with new, randomized vectors to produce novel outputs.
concepts.content:
To learn to synthesize realistic images, we start with a training set of examples of real images, $\{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$. In this context, an example is an {`input`, `output`} pair where the `input` is the null set. We feed these examples to a learner, which produces a generator function. Later, we may query the generator with new, randomized $\mathbf{z}$-vectors to produce novel outputs, a process called **sampling** from the model. This two-stage procedure is shown in @fig-generative_models-gen_model_training_vs_sampling:

(see figure: Learning and using a generator.)
concepts.motivation_md: Once a model has learned the underlying distribution of a dataset, we need a way to use that knowledge. Sampling allows us to 'draw' from that distribution to create new, never-before-seen examples.
concepts.recap_md: - Sampling involves inputting random noise into a trained generator to create new data.

concepts.title: Objective of Generative Modeling
concepts.one_liner: The objective of generative modeling is to create a generator that produces synthetic data identically distributed to the real training data.
concepts.content:
The objective of the learner is to create a generator that produces *synthetic* data, $\{\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$, that looks like the *real* data, $\{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$. There are different ways to define "looks like":

1. Synthetic data matches the real data in terms of certain marginal statistics (e.g., mean color, variance, or edge statistics).
2. Synthetic data has high probability under a density model fit to the real data.

The first approach works well when we only want to match certain properties. The second approach is better when we want to produce synthetic data that matches *all* statistics of the training examples. In practice, we may not be able to match all statistics due to limits of the model's capacity. To be precise, the goal of deep generative models is to produce synthetic data that is *identically distributed* as the training data, that is, we want $\hat{\mathbf{x}} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}$ where $p_{\texttt{data}}$ is the true process that produced the training data.
concepts.motivation_md: The goal is to capture the 'essence' of a dataset so perfectly that the model's creations are indistinguishable from real-world observations, effectively learning the underlying probability distribution of the data.
concepts.recap_md: - The goal is to produce synthetic data that is identically distributed as the training data.

concepts.title: Generalization in Generative Models
concepts.one_liner: A good generative model must generalize by producing synthetic samples that look like the training data without simply memorizing and regurgitating them.
concepts.content: A property of a good generative model is that it be a simple, or smooth, function, so that it generalizes to producing synthetic samples that look like the training data but are not identical to it. A generator that only regurgitates the training data is overfit in the same way a classifier that memorizes the training data is overfit. In both cases, the true goal is to fit the training data and to do so with a function that generalizes. While memorized training samples satisfy the goal of making synthetic data look real, they fail the requirement of generalization.
concepts.motivation_md: If a model only repeats what it has seen, it hasn't truly learned the 'rules' of the data. Generalization ensures the model can create novel content that follows the same patterns as the original data.
concepts.recap_md: - Generalization prevents the model from simply memorizing and regurgitating training examples.

concepts.title: Diffusion Model
concepts.one_liner: Diffusion models are a class of generative models that break the hard problem of image generation into many simple corruption and restoration steps.
concepts.content:
Diffusion models use a strategy similar to autoregressive models by breaking a hard problem into many simple pieces. They can be understood by looking at what autoregressive models do in the reverse direction: starting with a complete image, they remove one pixel, then the next, and the next.

(see figure: An autoregressive sequence in reverse is a corruption process that removes one pixel at a time.)
concepts.motivation_md: Generating complex data like high-resolution images in a single step is computationally difficult. Diffusion models solve this by decomposing the generation process into a sequence of small, manageable denoising steps, making the learning process more stable and effective.
concepts.recap_md: - Diffusion models break complex generation tasks into a series of simple steps. - They are conceptually related to autoregressive models viewed in a reverse corruption direction.

concepts.title: Reverse Diffusion Process
concepts.one_liner: The reverse diffusion process uses a neural network to learn the mapping from a noisier image back to a less noisy version.
concepts.content:
Just like autoregressive models, diffusion models train a neural net, $f_{\theta}$, to reverse the corruption process. It can be trained via supervised learning on example sequences of different images getting noisier and noisier. For example, as shown in the figure below, the sequence of images of a bird getting noisier can be flipped in time to provide a sequence of training examples of the mapping $\mathbf{x}_t \rightarrow \mathbf{x}_{t-1}$. These examples are then fit by a predictor $f_{\theta}$.

(see figure: Reverse diffusion process. The forward process creates supervision to train the reverse process.)
concepts.motivation_md: To generate data from noise, a model must learn how to undo the effects of corruption. By training on a reversed sequence of noise addition, the model learns to incrementally recover structure from chaos.

concepts.title: Denoiser
concepts.one_liner: A denoiser is a neural network that learns to remove small amounts of noise from an image to eventually recover a noise-less version.
concepts.content: We call $f_{\theta}$ a denoiser; it learns to remove a little bit of noise from an image. If we apply this denoiser over and over, starting with pure noise, the process should coalesce on a noise-less image that looks like one of our training examples.
concepts.motivation_md: The denoiser is the core functional unit of a diffusion model, responsible for the iterative refinement of data from a high-entropy state (noise) to a low-entropy state (a clean image).
concepts.recap_md: - The denoiser $f_{\theta}$ is trained to remove small increments of noise. - Repeated application of the denoiser transforms pure noise into a structured image.

concepts.title: Training Diffusion Models
concepts.one_liner: Training a diffusion model involves generating noisy data through a forward process and training a neural network to invert those steps.
concepts.content:
The steps to train a diffusion model are as follows:

1. Generate training data by corrupting a bunch of images (forward process; noising).
2. Train a neural net to invert each step of corruption (reverse process; denoising).

As an additional trick, it can help to let the denoising function observe time step $t$ as input, so that we have:
$$\begin{aligned} \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t-1} = f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_t, t) \end{aligned}$$
This can help the denoiser to make better predictions, because knowing $t$ helps us know if we are looking at a normal scene that has been corrupted by noise (likely if $t$ is large) or a scene where the actual physical structure is full of chaotic, rough textures that happen to look like noise (likely if $t$ is small, because for small $t$ we haven't added much noise yet).

(see figure: Training a diffusion model consists of first producing training pairs of the form {noisy image, less noisy image}. Then do supervised learning on these pairs.)
concepts.motivation_md: Standard supervised learning requires input-output pairs. By intentionally noising images, we create a synthetic dataset where the 'ground truth' is the less-noisy version, allowing us to train models to reverse the entropy increase.
concepts.recap_md: - Training involves a forward noising process and a reverse denoising process. - Including the time step $t$ as an input helps the model distinguish between added noise and natural image texture.

concepts.title: Probabilistic Interpretation of Diffusion Models
concepts.one_liner: Diffusion models can be interpreted probabilistically as Gaussian density models or variational autoencoders.
concepts.content: Diffusion models are trained using a loss $\mathcal{L}$, which could be the $L_2$ distance. In many diffusion models, $f_{\theta}$ is instead trained to output the parameters (mean and variance) as a Gaussian density model fit to the data. This formulation yields useful probabilistic interpretations; in fact, such a diffusion model can be framed as a variational autoencoder. However, diffusion models can still work well without these interpretations, instead using a wide variety of prediction models for $f_{\theta}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Framing diffusion models probabilistically allows researchers to use established tools from information theory and Bayesian inference, such as variational bounds, to improve and analyze model performance.
concepts.recap_md: - Models can be trained to output Gaussian parameters (mean and variance) rather than just a point estimate. - This approach allows diffusion models to be framed as variational autoencoders.

concepts.title: Noise Prediction Reparameterization
concepts.one_liner: A common training trick is to reparameterize the model to predict the noise added to an image rather than the clean signal itself.
concepts.content:
One useful trick for training diffusion models is to reparameterize the learning problem as predicting the noise rather than the signal:
$$\begin{aligned} f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_t, t) &= \epsilon_t &\quad\quad \triangleleft \quad\text{first predict noise}\\ \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t-1} &= \mathbf{x}_t + \epsilon_t &\quad\quad \triangleleft \quad\text{then remove this noise} \end{aligned}$$

concepts.title: Generative Adversarial Network (GAN)
concepts.one_liner: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) directly sample complex distributions in a single step by using a classifier to distinguish between real and synthetic data.
concepts.content: While autoregressive and diffusion models build up complex distributions step by step, the generative adversarial network (GAN) creates a system that directly outputs samples from the complex distribution in one step. The goal of generative modeling is to make synthetic data that looks like real data. GANs take a direct and intuitive approach: synthetic data looks like real data if a classifier cannot distinguish between synthetic images and real images.
concepts.motivation_md: GANs were developed to avoid the iterative sampling required by other models, aiming for a more direct 'one-shot' generation process driven by a competitive learning framework.

concepts.title: Reverse KL Divergence
concepts.one_liner: The reverse KL divergence, $\mathrm{KL}(p_\theta \| p_{\text {data }})$, measures the probability of the model's samples under the true data distribution.
concepts.content: $\mathrm{KL}(p_{\text {data }} \| p_\theta)$ is sometimes called the forward KL divergence, and it measures the probability of the data under the model distribution. The reverse KL divergence, $\mathrm{KL}(p_\theta \| p_{\text {data }})$, does the converse, measuring the probability of the model's samples under the data distribution. Because we do not have access to the true data distribution, the reverse KL divergence usually cannot be computed.
concepts.motivation_md: While forward KL divergence is standard for maximum likelihood, reverse KL divergence provides an alternative perspective by evaluating how likely model-generated samples are to have come from the real data distribution. It is a fundamental concept in variational inference and generative modeling, even if it is often intractable to compute directly.

concepts.title: Maximum Likelihood Learning for Density Models
concepts.one_liner: Maximum likelihood learning for density models attempts to increase the probability density at observed datapoints while implicitly decreasing it elsewhere.
concepts.content:
Maximizing the likelihood objective is a form of maximum likelihood learning. Pictorially, we can visualize this objective as trying to push up the density over each observed datapoint:

(see figure: Fitting a max likelihood density model to data. The gray region holds a constant amount of mass; think of it as piles of dirt. To increase the amount of dirt at the locations of the green arrows you...)

Remember that a probability density function (pdf) is a function $p_{\theta}: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow [0,\infty)$ with $\int_{\mathbf{x}} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})d\mathbf{x} = 1$. To learn a pdf, we typically learn the parameters of a family of pdfs, such as the Gaussian family. All members of such a family are normalized nonnegative functions; because they are normalized, whenever we push up density over datapoints, we are forced to sacrifice density over other regions. This implicitly removes density from places where there is no data.

concepts.title: Energy-Based Models (EBMs)
concepts.one_liner: Energy-based models (EBMs) learn an unnormalized function $E_\theta$ to represent data, avoiding the difficult constraint of ensuring the total probability integrates to one.
concepts.content:
Density models constrain the learned function to be normalized, such that $\int_{\mathbf{x}} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})d\mathbf{x} = 1$. This constraint is often hard to realize. One approach is to learn an unnormalized function $E_{\theta}$, then convert it to a normalized density. Note that low energy implies high probability; thus, we minimize energy to maximize probability.

Energy-based models (EBMs) address the normalization challenge by skipping the normalization step and letting the output of the learner just be $E_\theta$. Even though it is not a true probability density, $E_{\theta}$ can still be used for many applications because we can compare relative probabilities. In sum, energy functions can do most of what probability densities can do, except they do not give normalized probabilities. Therefore, they are insufficient for applications where communicating true probabilities is important for interpretability or interfacing with downstream systems, such as a medical imaging system communicating the likelihood of cancer.

concepts.title: Normalizing Constant (Partition Function)
concepts.one_liner: The normalizing constant $Z(\theta)$, or partition function, is the integral of the unnormalized density over all possible data values.
concepts.content: A density can be defined as $p_{\theta} = \frac{e^{-E_{\theta}}}{Z(\theta)}$, where $Z(\theta) = \int_{\mathbf{x}} e^{-E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})}d\mathbf{x}$ is the normalizing constant. The $Z(\theta)$ can be very expensive to compute and often can only be approximated. Notice that $Z$ is a function of model parameters $\theta$ but not of the datapoint $\mathbf{x}$, since we integrate over all possible data values.
concepts.motivation_md: To turn an arbitrary non-negative function into a valid probability distribution, we must divide by the sum (or integral) of all its possible values so that the total probability equals one.

concepts.title: Contrastive Divergence
concepts.one_liner: Contrastive divergence is an optimization method for energy-based models that modifies the energy function to decrease energy for data samples and increase it for model samples.
concepts.content:
Contrastive divergence is a method that modifies the energy function on each iteration of optimization to decrease the energy assigned to samples from the data (positive term) and to increase the energy assigned to samples from the model (negative term):

(see figure: Fitting a max likelihood energy function to data, using contrastive divergence. @hinton2002training)

Once the energy function perfectly adheres to the data, samples from the model are identical to samples from the data and the positive and negative terms cancel out. Mathematically, this procedure approximates the gradient of the log likelihood function. Defining $p_{\theta} = \frac{e^{-E_{\theta}}}{Z(\theta)}$, we decompose the gradient of the log likelihood:

$$\begin{aligned} \nabla_{\theta} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}[\log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})] &= -\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}[\nabla_{\theta} E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})] - \nabla_{\theta} \log Z(\theta) \end{aligned}$$

The first term is the positive term gradient. The second term, the negative term gradient, is an intractable integral that we rewrite as an expectation to be approximated via sampling:

$$\begin{aligned} \nabla_{\theta} \log Z(\theta) &= -\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\theta}}[\nabla_{\theta} E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})] \end{aligned}$$

Plugging this back in, we arrive at:

$$\begin{aligned} \nabla_{\theta} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}[\log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})] &= -\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}[\nabla_{\theta}E_{\theta(\mathbf{x})}] + \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\theta}}[\nabla_{\theta} E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})] \end{aligned}$$

By taking $N$ samples $\mathbf{x}^{(i)} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}$ and $\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)} \sim p_{\theta}$, we approximate the gradient as $\frac{1}{N} \nabla_{\theta} \sum_{i=1}^N (-E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}) + E_{\theta}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)}))$. This establishes a contrast between data and model samples, bringing the model closer to the data. Contrastive divergence is an optimizer specifically built for max likelihood objectives over energy functions.

concepts.title: Comparing Different Kinds of Generative Models
concepts.one_liner: Generative models can be categorized by whether they provide density functions, energy functions, or generator functions.
concepts.content:
Generative models can be summarized by whether they produce density functions $p_{\theta}: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow [0,\infty)$, energy functions $E_{\theta}: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, or generators $g_{\theta}: \mathcal{Z} \rightarrow \mathcal{X}$. Each family has distinct trade-offs. Generators utilize latent variables $\mathbf{z}$ to control properties of the generated output, allowing meaningful changes by varying these inputs. In contrast, density and energy models lack direct latent control but provide scores related to data likelihood, which are useful for anomaly detection or synthesizing high-quality data through optimization.

Models are roughly categorized by their straightforward usage, though some properties can be added with extra effort (e.g., sampling from a density model or estimating density from a VAE). 

| Method | Latents? | Density/Energy? | Generator? |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Energy-based models | ❌ | ✅ (energy only) | ❌|
| Gaussian | ❌ | ✅ | ❌|
| Autoregressive models | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ (slow) |
| Diffusion models | ✅ (high-dimensional) | ❌ | ✅ (slow) |
| GANs | ✅ | ❌ | ✅ |
| VAEs | ✅ | ❌ | ✅ |

Generative models also differ in their objectives, hypothesis spaces, and optimization algorithms. Some, like autoregressive models, refer to a hypothesis space, while others, like VAEs, refer to a specific conjunction of objective, hypothesis space, and optimization algorithm.

concepts.title: Gaussian Density Model
concepts.one_liner: The Gaussian distribution is a simple density model defined by its mean and variance parameters.
concepts.content: One of the simplest and most useful density models is the Gaussian distribution, which in one dimension (1D) is: $$p_{\theta}(x) = \frac{1}{Z}e^{-(x-\theta_1)^2/(2\theta_2)}$$ This density has two parameters, $\theta_1$ (mean) and $\theta_2$ (variance). The normalization constant $Z$ ensures the function is normalized. The typical strategy in defining density models is to create a parameterized family of functions where every member is normalized, then search over the parameters to optimize a generative modeling objective.

concepts.title: Maximum Likelihood Objective for Density Models
concepts.one_liner: The maximum likelihood objective for density models seeks to maximize the expected log-probability of the data.
concepts.content: For density models, the most common objective is maximum likelihood: $$\mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}[\log p_{\theta}(x)] \approx \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \log p_{\theta}(x^{(i)})$$ This objective measures how well the model's probability distribution aligns with the observed data samples.

concepts.title: Maximum Likelihood Estimation for 1D Gaussian
concepts.one_liner: Maximum likelihood estimation for a 1D Gaussian results in setting the parameters to the empirical mean and variance of the data.
concepts.content:
For a 1D Gaussian, the log-likelihood objective takes the form: $$\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \log \frac{1}{Z}e^{-(x^{(i)}-\theta_1)^2/(2\theta_2)} = -\log(Z) + \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N (x^{(i)}-\theta_1)^2/(2\theta_2)$$ While optimization can be done via gradient descent, an analytical solution exists by setting the gradient to zero. For the mean $\theta_1^*$, the solution is the empirical mean: $$\theta_1^* = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N x^{(i)}$$ For the variance $\theta_2^*$, noting that $\frac{\partial (-\log Z)}{\partial \theta_2^*} = \frac{1}{2\theta_2^*}$, the solution is the empirical variance: $$\theta_2^* = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N (x^{(i)}-\theta_1^*)^2$$ This shows that to maximize the probability of the data under a Gaussian, one should set the model parameters to the data's empirical mean and variance.

concepts.title: Autoregressive Model
concepts.one_liner: Autoregressive models synthesize data sequentially, predicting each new element based on the previously generated sequence.
concepts.content:
An autoregressive model synthesizes an image pixel by pixel, where each new pixel is decided based on the sequence already generated. This is treated as a sequence prediction problem: given a sequence of observed pixels, a learned function $f_{\theta}$ predicts the color of the next one. 

As shown in (see figure: An autoregressive model, f_{\theta}, that generates an image pixel by pixel. The black pixels are the remaining pixels to synthesize. Compare with the Efros-Leung model in @fig-sampling_efros_leung.), the model predicts each next pixel from a partial image. The context is the region the prediction is based on, which could be the entire synthesized image or a smaller window. After predicting the distribution for the next pixel, a color is chosen—either the most likely or by sampling to introduce randomness—and the context window slides forward to repeat the process.
concepts.motivation_md: Autoregressive models simplify the complex task of high-dimensional data generation by breaking it down into a series of simpler conditional 1D prediction steps.
concepts.recap_md: - Data is generated sequentially, with each step conditioned on a 'context' of previous outputs.

concepts.title: Categorical Distribution for Pixel Modeling
concepts.one_liner: A categorical distribution can fully represent the probability mass function of a single grayscale pixel's 256 possible values.
concepts.content: Synthesizing a single grayscale pixel is straightforward because it can take on one of 256 possible values (for standard 8-bit images). A categorical distribution is used to represent the probability of each value. This distribution is fully expressive, meaning it can represent any possible probability mass function (pmf) over those 256 values. Fitting the distribution to training data involves counting the frequency of each value in the training set and normalizing by the total count. Once fit, we can sample from this distribution to synthesize a random one-pixel image.
concepts.motivation_md: Using a categorical distribution for pixels avoids making assumptions about the shape of the color distribution, allowing the model to learn any arbitrary frequency of pixel intensities from the data.
concepts.recap_md: - Grayscale pixels are modeled as categorical variables with 256 possible outcomes.

concepts.title: Next-pixel Softmax Regression
concepts.one_liner: Modeling the distribution of the next pixel in a sequence can be treated as a 256-way softmax regression problem conditioned on previous observations.
concepts.content: To model the distribution over a second grayscale pixel given the first, we model $p(\mathbf{x_2} \bigm | \mathbf{x_1})$ where $\mathbf{x_1}$ is the first pixel and $\mathbf{x_2}$ is the second. In this context, we index the first pixel as $\mathbf{x}_1$ rather than $\mathbf{x}_0$. Treating $\mathbf{x}_2$ as a categorical variable, we can use a softmax regression, as seen in @sec-intro_to_learning-image_classification. While that section modeled a $K$-way categorical distribution over object classes, we can use the same tools to model a 256-way distribution over the second pixel in a sequence. This logic extends via induction: modeling each next pixel in the sequence is a softmax regression problem that models $p(\mathbf{x}_n \bigm | \mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_{n-1})$. The cross-entropy loss can be computed as shown in (see figure: Autoregressive prediction as next-pixel-classification.). This process looks almost identical to the diagram in @fig-softmax_regression_diagram from @sec-intro_to_learning.
concepts.motivation_md: This technique allows us to apply well-understood supervised learning tools, like softmax regression and cross-entropy loss, to the complex task of generative modeling by framing image generation as a sequence of classification problems.
concepts.recap_md: - Each pixel is treated as a categorical variable with 256 possible intensity values. - The model predicts the probability of the next pixel conditioned on all previously observed pixels in the sequence. - Standard cross-entropy loss is used to train the model to predict the correct pixel values.

concepts.title: Pixel Sequence Ordering
concepts.one_liner: Images can be modeled as sequences by vectorizing the 2D grid of pixels, typically by listing them row by row.
concepts.content: To model color images, we predict three values per pixel for the red, green, and blue channels in sequence. This involves predicting the red value as a 256-way classification problem, sampling it, and then predicting the green and blue values. To turn an image into a sequence of pixels, the simplest method is to vectorize the 2D grid by listing the first row of pixels, then the second row, and so forth. While any fixed ordering of the pixels into a sequence is valid, this simple raster-scan method is the most common.
concepts.motivation_md: Autoregressive models require a sequential input, so a consistent method for flattening 2D or 3D image data into a 1D sequence is necessary for the model to learn spatial dependencies.
concepts.recap_md: - Color images are handled by sequencing the red, green, and blue channels for each pixel. - The most common ordering method is raster order, which processes pixels row by row. - Any fixed sequence ordering is valid for defining the conditional dependencies in the model.

concepts.title: Chain Rule of Probability
concepts.one_liner: The chain rule of probability allows any joint distribution to be factorized into a product of conditional distributions.
concepts.content: According to the chain rule of probability, any joint distribution can be factorized into a product of conditionals as follows: $$\begin{aligned} p(\mathbf{X}) &= p(\mathbf{x_n} \bigm | \mathbf{x_1}, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_{n-1})p(\mathbf{x}_{n-1} \bigm | \mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_{n-2}) \quad \ldots \quad p(\mathbf{x}_2 \bigm | \mathbf{x}_1)p(\mathbf{x}_1) \\ p(\mathbf{X}) &= \prod_{i=1}^n p(\mathbf{x}_i \bigm | \mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_{i-1}) \end{aligned}$$ As a notational convenience, we define $p(\mathbf{x}_i \mid \mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_{i-1}) = p(\mathbf{x}_1)$ when $i=1$.
concepts.motivation_md: This rule provides the mathematical foundation for autoregressive models, enabling the decomposition of a complex high-dimensional joint distribution into a series of simpler, learnable conditional distributions.
concepts.recap_md: - Any joint probability distribution can be expressed as a product of conditional probabilities. - The probability of the first element is defined as the base case for the product. - This factorization justifies predicting sequences one element at a time.

concepts.title: Training Autoregressive Models
concepts.one_liner: Training an autoregressive model involves extracting supervised input-output pairs of pixel sequences and their corresponding next pixels from training images.

For a pixel-based model, this means extracting sequences of pixels $\mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_{n-1}$ and the corresponding observed next pixel $\mathbf{x}_n$. These can be extracted by traversing training images in raster order. The full training and testing setup is shown in (see figure: Training an autoregressive model, then sampling images from it.).

concepts.title: Type 1 Training Batch (Independent Sequences)
concepts.one_liner: A type 1 training batch consists of independent sequence and completion pairs sampled from random starting locations in different random images.
concepts.content: One way to create a training batch is the type 1 batch: $$\begin{aligned} &\texttt{input}: \mathbf{x}_k^{(i)}, \dots, \mathbf{x}_{k+n-1}^{(i)} \quad\quad \texttt{target output}: \mathbf{x}_{k+n}^{(i)} \\ &\texttt{input}: \mathbf{x}_l^{(j)}, \dots, \mathbf{x}_{l+n-1}^{(j)} \quad\quad \texttt{target output}: \mathbf{x}_{l+n}^{(j)} \end{aligned}$$ In this setup, we sample supervised [sequence, completion] pairs that each come from a different random starting location (indexed by $k$ and $l$) in a different random image (indexed by $i$ and $j$).
concepts.motivation_md: This method ensures that the training batch is diverse and that the model sees a wide variety of contexts and starting points across the dataset.
concepts.recap_md: - Each example in the batch is an independent sequence and its next-token target. - Sequences are sampled from random images and random starting positions. - This approach provides a straightforward way to construct supervised training batches.

concepts.title: Type 2 Training Batch (Overlapping Sequences)
concepts.one_liner: Type 2 training batches use overlapping sequences to share computations, making the training process significantly more efficient.
concepts.content: Another way to set up batches is the type 2 batch, where the example sequences overlap: $$\begin{aligned} &\texttt{input}: \mathbf{x}_1^{(i)}, \dots, \mathbf{x}_{n-1}^{(i)} \quad\quad \texttt{target output}: \mathbf{x}_n^{(i)} \\ &\texttt{input}: \mathbf{x}_2^{(i)}, \dots, \mathbf{x}_{n}^{(i)} \quad\quad \texttt{target output}: \mathbf{x}_{n+1}^{(i)} \end{aligned}$$ This method is much more efficient because the representations computed for predicting $\mathbf{x}_n$ from $\mathbf{x}_1, \dots, \mathbf{x}_{n-1}$ can be reused for predicting the next item, $\mathbf{x}_{n+1}$. This is particularly useful in architectures like transformers with causal attention (@sec-transformers-masked_attention), where the representation of an item only depends on its predecessors. This allows the model to share computation between all overlapping predictions, as described in @eq-transformers-causal_training_batches.
concepts.motivation_md: Sequential prediction is computationally expensive; overlapping batches allow models to reuse intermediate calculations, drastically reducing the total compute required to process a dataset.
concepts.recap_md: - Training examples consist of overlapping segments from the same sequence. - Reusing hidden state representations across overlapping steps increases computational efficiency. - This batching style is standard for training transformers with causal masking.

concepts.title: Direct Approach to Generative Modeling
concepts.one_liner: The direct approach to generative modeling learns the function $G: \mathcal{Z} \rightarrow \mathcal{X}$ to map latent variables to data.
concepts.content: There are two general approaches to forming data generators. The direct approach involves learning the function $G: \mathcal{Z} \rightarrow \mathcal{X}$. In the generative modeling literature, the direct approach is sometimes called an implicit model because the probability density is never explicitly represented. However, this model explicitly describes the way data is generated. The direct approach has recently become popular with models like generative adversarial networks (GANs) and diffusion models, as schematized in @fig-generative_models-gen_model_training_vs_sampling.
concepts.motivation_md: The direct approach simplifies generative modeling by learning a straight mapping from a simple noise source to complex data. This avoids the need to explicitly define or compute complex probability densities, enabling the high-fidelity synthesis seen in modern GANs and diffusion models.

concepts.one_liner: Density models are generative models that yield a probability density function $p_{\theta}$ fit to the training data.
concepts.content: Some generative models not only produce generators but also yield a probability density function $p_{\theta}$, fit to the training data. Some generative models only produce a density $p_{\theta}$ and do not learn any explicit generator function; instead, samples can be drawn from $p_{\theta}$ using a sampling algorithm that takes a density as input and produces samples from it as output. concepts.title: Divergence between Distributions
concepts.one_liner: A divergence measures the closeness between two distributions and is defined by nonnegativity and the property that $D(p,q) = 0 \iff p=q$.
concepts.content: To measure closeness between a model distribution $p_{\theta}$ and the data distribution $p_{\texttt{data}}$, we can define a divergence $D$ and solve the optimization problem $\mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_{p_\theta} D(p_{\theta}, p_{\texttt{data}})$. Since we only have samples $\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}$, we need a divergence $D$ that measures the distance between $p_{\theta}$ and $p_{\texttt{data}}$ while only accessing samples. A divergence need not be a proper distance metric; it can be nonsymmetric and need not satisfy the triangle inequality. It is defined by just two properties: nonnegativity and $D(p,q) = 0 \iff p=q$.
concepts.motivation_md: In generative modeling, we need a way to quantify how closely our model's distribution matches the true data distribution. Since we only have access to samples of the real data, we require a mathematical measure—a divergence—that can be estimated from those samples to guide the optimization process.

concepts.title: Kullback-Leibler (KL) Divergence
concepts.one_liner: The Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence is a measure of distribution closeness that, when minimized, is equivalent to maximizing the expected log likelihood of the training data.
concepts.content: A common choice for measuring distribution closeness is the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence, defined as follows: $$\begin{aligned} p_{\theta}^* &= \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_{p_\theta} \mathrm{KL}\left(p_{\text {data }} \| p_\theta\right)\\ &= \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_{p_\theta} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}\Big[-\log \frac{p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})}{p_{\texttt{data}}(\mathbf{x})}\Big]\\ &= \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}_{p_\theta} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}\big[\log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})\big] - \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}\big[\log p_{\texttt{data}}(\mathbf{x})\big]\\ &= \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}_{p_\theta} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}\big[\log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})\big] \quad \triangleleft \quad\text{dropped second term since no dependence on $p_{\theta}$} \\ &\approx \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}_{p_\theta} \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}) \end{aligned}$$ The final line is an empirical estimate of the expectation by sampling over the training dataset. This is the expected log likelihood of the training data under the model's density function. $\mathrm{KL}\left(p_{\text {data }} \| p_\theta\right)$ is sometimes called the forward KL divergence, measuring the probability of the data under the model distribution, while the reverse KL divergence $\mathrm{KL}\left(p_\theta \| p_{\text {data }}\right)$ measures the probability of the model's samples under the data distribution.
concepts.motivation_md: KL divergence provides a principled information-theoretic way to measure the difference between distributions. Its forward form is particularly useful because it simplifies into the maximum likelihood objective, which is the standard method for fitting statistical models to observed data.

concepts.one_liner: A discriminator is a function $d_{\phi}$ that attempts to classify whether data is synthesized by a generator or comes from a real dataset.

concepts.title: GAN Minimax Game
concepts.one_liner: GAN training is a minimax game where a generator tries to fool a discriminator while the discriminator learns to detect synthetic data.
concepts.content: The generator $g_{\theta}$ and discriminator $d_{\phi}$ play an adversarial game in which $g_{\theta}$ tries to become better at generating synthetic images while $d_{\phi}$ tries to become better at detecting errors $g_{\theta}$ is making. The learning problem can be written as a minimax game: $$\begin{aligned} \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_\theta\max_\phi \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}[\log d_{\phi}(\mathbf{x})] + \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z} \sim p_{\mathbf{z}}}[\log (1-d_{\phi}(g_{\theta}(\mathbf{z})))] \end{aligned}$$. Schematically, the generator synthesizes images that are then fed as input to the discriminator. The discriminator tries to assign a high score to generated images (classifying them as synthetic) and a low score to real images from some training set (classifying them as real). (see figure: Architecture of a GAN being trained to generate images of flamingos. The synthetic image in this example is generated by BigGAN @brock2018large)

concepts.title: Alternating Gradient Descent for GANs
concepts.one_liner: GAN optimization alternates between updating the discriminator to maximize classification accuracy and updating the generator to minimize it.
concepts.content: Given a particular generator $g_{\theta}$, $d_{\phi}$ tries to maximize its ability to discriminate between real and synthetic images. The objective of $d_{\phi}$ is logistic regression between a set of real data $\{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$ and synthetic data $\{\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$, where $\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)} = g_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}^{(i)})$. The optimal discriminator $d_{\phi}^*$ is defined as: $$\begin{aligned} d_{\phi}^* = \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}_{\phi} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}[\log d_{\phi}(\mathbf{x})] + \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z} \sim p_{\mathbf{z}}}[\log (1-d_{\phi}(g_{\theta}(\mathbf{z})))] \end{aligned}$$. From the perspective of $g_{\theta}$, it tries to solve: $$\begin{aligned} \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_{\theta} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z} \sim p_{\mathbf{z}}}[\log (1-d_{\phi}^*(g_{\theta}(\mathbf{z})))] \end{aligned}$$. Because $d_{\phi}^*$ depends on the current behavior of $g_{\theta}$, updating the generator requires re-solving for the discriminator. To optimize a GAN, we alternate between taking one gradient step on the generator objective and $K$ gradient steps on the discriminator objective. In practice, setting $K=1$ is often sufficient.

concepts.title: GANs as Statistical Image Models
concepts.one_liner: GANs are learned statistical image models that amortize the optimization of matching data statistics by learning a mapping from latent noise to samples.
concepts.content: GANs are related to statistical image and texture models where images are synthesized with the same statistics as a source texture. In traditional models like Heeger-Bergen, this is an optimization problem where pixels are adjusted until subband histograms match a training image. In the language of GANs, the loss checking for such a match is a kind of discriminator, but it is hand-defined rather than learned. Additionally, GANs amortize the optimization via learning; they learn a mapping $g_{\theta}$ from latent noise to samples rather than arriving at samples via an optimization process that starts from scratch each time a new sample is needed.
